what_it_does: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a technique for building realistic 3D scenes from photos; training it on a small edge device (like a laptop or embedded board) is very slow because the rendering step requires processing overlapping fuzzy blobs in a strict depth order — nearest blob first — which forces sequential computation and prevents the hardware from working on many blobs at once. Local-GS sidesteps this by switching to an order-independent rendering method, meaning blobs can be processed in any sequence, which breaks the dependency chain and lets the hardware schedule many pixel-intersection tests in parallel based on which blobs are physically nearby. A set of unified hardware cores handles both the forward rendering pass and the backward gradient pass (needed to update the model during training) simultaneously, improving how much of the chip stays busy. The paper claims this enables practical 3DGS training on memory-constrained edge hardware, though detailed measurements are not available from the abstract.
